intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, shows how to remember it and warns where people slip. Work the section exercises with a pencil, answer the recall questions before you look, and keep a real budget document open beside you as you read.

sections.title: What Public Finance Is About
sections.big_idea: The budget states in numbers what a government values. Public finance does **three jobs**: allocate, redistribute and stabilise.
in_plain_words: Musgrave's three functions give you the first frame. The state allocates goods that markets under-supply, redistributes income and assets through taxes and transfers, and steers the economy through the cycle. In practice one decision, like a food subsidy, touches all three.

Markets under-supply public goods, spillovers and services with information problems, which is the reason for spending. The deck says the real political contest is over which interventions, at what scale and with what design. The state also plays four roles: provider, payer, regulator and absent.

diagram.caption: the market failure reasons on slide 6

key_terms.meaning: Providing goods and services that markets under-supply.
Redistributing income and assets through taxes, transfers and targeted spending.
Managing the macro economy across the cycle.
Non-rival and non-excludable, so markets under-supply it.
A spillover on others, such as pollution or a vaccination benefit.

worked_example.title: Who spends the public rupee?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: take ₹100 of public spending and apply the deck's rough shares. Half happens at State level and about 5% at local level.
steps: State level: 100 × 0.5 = 50.
Local level: 100 × 0.05 = 5.
What remains for the Union, if those shares hold: 100 − 50 − 5 = 45.
Check against slide 4: State budgets together exceed Union spending, and 50 is more than 45.
worked_example.answer: About ₹50 at State level, ₹5 local and ₹45 Union, in line with the deck's claim that States spend more than the Union.

mistakes: Giving a measure one label. A food subsidy allocates, distributes and stabilises at once, so name all three.
Calling a good public because the state provides it. Check whether it is non-rival and non-excludable.
Reading the budget as a technical exercise when the deck treats it as a contested political compromise.

recall.q: Name Musgrave's three functions.
recall.a: Allocation, distribution and stabilisation.

recall.q: What two tests define a public good?
recall.a: Non-rival and non-excludable.

recall.q: Which four roles does the state play in the public-private mix?
recall.a: Direct provider, payer, regulator and absent.

recall.q: What should you be able to do by the end of the deck?
recall.a: Read Budget at a Glance, locate a scheme in the Demand for Grants and say which level of government finances what.

recall.q: What is the practitioner test on slide 4?
recall.a: Can you name a programme's budget head, last year's releases and its demand for grants.

sections.title: Indian Fiscal Structure
sections.big_idea: Before you read a number, learn the **containers, categories and deficits** it sits in. Four questions cover most of any budget document.
in_plain_words: Public money lives in three places. The Consolidated Fund needs Parliament's appropriation, the Public Account holds money the government keeps as banker, and the Contingency Fund covers the unforeseen. Articles 110 to 117 and 265 to 267 are the legal frame, and the CAG audits afterwards.

Receipts split into tax, non-tax, borrowing and non-debt capital, and spending splits into revenue and capital. Then three deficits measure borrowing from three angles: revenue deficit, fiscal deficit and primary deficit. Read all three together.

diagram.note: primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments

key_terms.meaning: Main legal home of public money under Art. 266(1); spending needs appropriation.
Money held as banker, such as provident funds; no appropriation needed.
Spending inside the Consolidated Fund that Parliament debates but cannot vote down.
Revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts.
Fiscal deficit minus interest payments.

worked_example.title: Three deficits from one set of figures
worked_example.setup: Illustrative figures in ₹ lakh crore, using the deck's definitions. Total expenditure 100, of which revenue expenditure 85. Revenue receipts 70, non-debt capital receipts 5, interest payments 18.
steps: Revenue deficit: 85 − 70 = 15.
Receipts without borrowing: 70 + 5 = 75.
Fiscal deficit: 100 − 75 = 25.
Primary deficit: 25 − 18 = 7.
worked_example.answer: Revenue deficit 15, fiscal deficit 25 and primary deficit 7. Interest takes up most of the borrowing, so past debt shapes the picture.

mistakes: Treating borrowing as a receipt on a par with tax revenue. It creates a future obligation.
Asking whether money is in 'the budget' without asking whether it sits in the Consolidated Fund or the Public Account.
Reading one deficit alone. A high fiscal deficit with a low primary deficit signals a debt-trap pattern.

recall.q: Which article creates the Contingency Fund?
recall.a: Article 267.

recall.q: What is the difference between charged and voted expenditure?
recall.a: Charged items, such as interest, are debated but cannot be voted down; everything else is voted through the Demands for Grants.

recall.q: Name the three audit types of the CAG.
recall.a: Financial, compliance and performance.

recall.q: How is the fiscal deficit defined?
recall.a: Total expenditure minus revenue receipts and non-debt capital receipts.

recall.q: What are the four first questions for any budget document?
recall.a: Which fund, which authority appropriates, which receipt category and how the deficit numbers move.

sections.title: Union Budget: How It's Made
sections.big_idea: The budget is a **twelve-month cycle** with several entry points for advocacy, and the documents differ in what they tell you.
in_plain_words: The cycle starts in August with a circular from the Department of Economic Affairs and ends with audit in the following year. Presentation on 1 February, committee scrutiny in February and March, and passage of the Appropriation and Finance Bills by 31 March fall in between.

Four special procedures handle money outside the normal route, and the FRBM Act is the statute for discipline. Open Budget Survey scores show documents are available but public participation is low. That gap is where advocacy has room.

key_terms.meaning: Ministry-wise estimates voted by Lok Sabha.
Art. 116 authority to spend before the full Budget passes.
Extra money sought during the year under Art. 115.
Retrospective approval for spending beyond the authorised amount.
Departmentally-Related Standing Committee shadowing a cluster of Ministries.

worked_example.title: Pick the right procedure
worked_example.setup: Four situations arise in a financial year. Match each to a mechanism from slide 21, then count a committee's members.
steps: A general election means the full Budget cannot pass before 1 April: Vote on Account.
A Ministry needs more than it was voted: Supplementary Demand.
Spending already exceeded what was authorised: Excess Demand, sought after CAG audit.
A new scheme needs nominal approval before real spending: Token Demand.
Each DRSC has 21 Lok Sabha and 10 Rajya Sabha members: 21 + 10 = 31.
worked_example.answer: Vote on Account, Supplementary, Excess and Token Demand in that order, and 31 members per committee.

mistakes: Starting with the Budget Speech. The deck's practitioner starting point is Budget at a Glance.
Ignoring committee reports. The deck says most substantive parliamentary scrutiny happens there.
Assuming supplementary demands are always a problem. They are routine, and only frequent large ones on one head are a signal.

recall.q: When did the Budget date move to 1 February?
How many DRSCs are there and how are they split?
recall.a: Twenty-four: 16 attached to Lok Sabha and 8 to Rajya Sabha.

recall.q: What did the 2018 FRBM amendment change?
recall.a: It moved to a debt anchor of 40 percent of GDP for the Centre and 60 percent combined, with the fiscal deficit at 3 percent.

recall.q: What was India's Open Budget Survey 2023 score for public participation?
recall.a: 6 out of 100.

recall.q: Which document is the Finance Minister's political statement?
recall.a: The Budget Speech.

sections.title: Tax Policy in India
sections.big_idea: The state can only spend what its tax system finances, and India's **tax-GDP ratio has stayed at 16 to 18 percent** for two decades.
in_plain_words: Direct taxes are progressive in design while indirect taxes tend to be regressive, because the poor spend more of their income on consumption. Income tax reaches few people, GST is a shared tax run by a Council, and corporate tax was cut in 2019.

Cess and surcharge let the Centre keep revenue outside the divisible pool. Behind it all sits a narrow base: informal work, an agricultural income exemption and weak property tax. The deck says most reforms have been recommended for decades and implemented only in part.

left.title: Direct tax
items: Burden falls on the person liable

right.title: Indirect tax
items: Burden passed to consumers via prices

key_terms.meaning: Tax revenue as a share of GDP; India's is roughly 16 to 18 percent.
Art. 279A body; decisions need a three-fourths weighted majority.
A purpose-specific levy that stays outside the divisible pool.
An extra levy on a tax, also outside the divisible pool.
Minimum Alternate Tax at 15 percent on book profits.

worked_example.title: What a rise in the ratio is worth
worked_example.setup: Slide 31 says a 2 to 3 point rise would add ₹6 to 9 lakh crore a year. Work out the GDP those figures imply.
steps: At a 2 point rise: 6 ÷ 0.02 = 300.
At a 3 point rise: 9 ÷ 0.03 = 300.
Both give about ₹300 lakh crore of GDP, so the slide's two ends agree.
Corporate rate cut of 2019: 30 − 22 = 8 percentage points.
worked_example.answer: The slide's range implies GDP of about ₹300 lakh crore, and the 2019 corporate cut was 8 percentage points.

mistakes: Quoting the tax-GDP ratio for the Centre alone. The slide's figure is Centre plus States.
Assuming the GST Council decides by simple majority. It needs three-fourths of the weighted vote.
Treating the 2019 corporate cut as proven to have paid for itself. The deck calls that empirically contested.

recall.q: Under which amendment did GST begin and when?
recall.a: The 101st Amendment, in force from 1 July 2017.

recall.q: What GST rates apply since 22 September 2025?
recall.a: 0, 5 and 18 percent, with a 40 percent rate on sin and luxury goods.

recall.q: What was the headline corporate rate before and after September 2019?
recall.a: 30 percent before and 22 percent after.

recall.q: Why do cess and surcharge matter to States?
recall.a: They stay outside the divisible pool, so a larger share of cess and surcharge means less devolution.

recall.q: Name two causes of India's narrow tax base.
recall.a: Any two of: a large informal economy, the agricultural income exemption, weak property tax, no wealth or inheritance tax.

sections.title: Fiscal Federalism & the Finance Commission
sections.big_idea: The Centre holds the rich tax bases, States hold the delivery, and the **Finance Commission bridges the gap** every five years.
in_plain_words: The Seventh Schedule gives the Centre income, corporate and customs taxes, while States have alcohol, land revenue and a narrower set. Each Finance Commission decides two things: the States' share of the divisible pool (vertical) and how it is split among States (horizontal).

The 15th FC formula weights income distance at 45 percent. The shift to 2011 population triggered the North-South debate. Centrally Sponsored Schemes are a second, conditional channel. The GST compensation episode showed how fragile the bargain is when the Centre's discretion decides.

key_terms.meaning: Net central taxes after cess, surcharge and collection costs, shared with States.
The States' collective share of the pool: 42% (14th FC), 41% (15th).
How the States' share is split among individual States.
Union-designed, jointly funded, State-executed.
Levy on demerit and luxury goods that funded the GST guarantee.

worked_example.title: Share of the pool, and a CSS split
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a divisible pool of ₹100 and a State whose horizontal share is 4%. Then a ₹100 scheme on a 60:40 split.
steps: The 15th FC's weights must total 100. The first three: 45 + 15 + 15 = 75.
Vertical share at 41%: 100 × 0.41 = 41.
The State's slice at 4%: 41 × 0.04 = 1.64.
A ₹100 scheme at 60:40: the Centre pays 100 × 0.6 = 60 and the State 100 − 60 = 40.
worked_example.answer: States share ₹41 of the pool, this State gets ₹1.64, and the CSS costs the Centre ₹60 and the State ₹40.

mistakes: Mixing up vertical and horizontal devolution. One is Centre against States and the other is State against State.
Assuming Finance Commission advice is binding. It has been accepted with minimal change but is not binding.
Treating all schemes as Centre-funded. A Central Sector Scheme is, and a CSS needs State contribution.

recall.q: What vertical share did the 14th and 15th FCs give States?
recall.a: 42 percent and 41 percent.

recall.q: Which criterion has the largest weight in the 15th FC formula?
recall.a: Income distance, at 45 percent.

recall.q: Why was the move to 2011 population contested?
recall.a: States with lower population growth, mostly in the south, see their share fall.

recall.q: What funding ratio applies to North-East schemes?
When did the GST compensation regime end?
recall.a: June 2022.

sections.title: State Finances & Sub-National Stress
sections.big_idea: States deliver most of what citizens meet as government, with **limited revenue, capped borrowing and growing commitments**.
in_plain_words: Devolution and central grants together fill about half of State receipts, and own revenue relies on alcohol, petroleum VAT and stamp duty. Article 293 lets the Centre cap borrowing, which is why off-budget routes and the Kerala case matter.

Stress shows up in four places: DISCOM losses, rising debt, pension commitments and cash-transfer schemes. The deck gives four markers for a State in active stress. Read the budget, the CAG audit, the MTFPS and the RBI chapter for your State.

key_terms.meaning: Requires Centre's consent for State borrowing while any sum is owed to the Centre.
State-owned electricity distribution company.
2015 scheme in which States took over 75% of DISCOM debt.
Defined-benefit pension against defined-contribution pension.
Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement under a State FRBM Act.

worked_example.title: Test a State against the markers
worked_example.setup: Illustrative State with revenue receipts of ₹200 crore and interest payments of ₹34 crore. Then apply the UDAY figures from slide 45.
steps: Interest share: 34 ÷ 200 = 0.17, which is 17 percent.
The marker is interest above 15 percent of revenue receipts, so this State crosses it.
UDAY: States took over 75 percent of about ₹4.3 lakh crore, so 4.3 × 0.75 = 3.225.
That is roughly ₹3.2 lakh crore moved onto State balance sheets.
worked_example.answer: The State crosses the interest marker at 17 percent, and UDAY moved about ₹3.2 lakh crore of DISCOM debt onto States.

mistakes: Judging a State by headline debt alone. Check all four markers: revenue deficit, interest share, pensions and off-budget liabilities.
Treating cash-transfer schemes as pure waste or pure gain. The deck says effects vary with scale and design.
Ignoring off-budget borrowing in State comparisons. It was used to circumvent ceilings.

recall.q: Why can the Centre control State borrowing in practice?
recall.a: Under Art. 293(3) consent is needed while any sum is owed to the Centre, which is almost always.

recall.q: What was the 15th FC target for combined State debt-to-GDP?
recall.a: 20 percent by 2025-26, which is off track.

recall.q: What four markers signal active fiscal stress?
recall.a: Persistent revenue deficit, interest above 15 percent of revenue receipts, a sharply rising pension burden and off-budget liabilities.

recall.q: What is the Unified Pension Scheme?
recall.a: The Centre's 2024 hybrid that guarantees 50 percent of average salary while keeping contributions.

recall.q: Which States reverted to OPS since 2022?
recall.a: Rajasthan, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Punjab and Himachal Pradesh.

sections.title: Local Government Finance
sections.big_idea: The 73rd and 74th Amendments gave local bodies functions on paper, but the **3F gap** of functions, finances and functionaries remains.
in_plain_words: Panchayats have 29 listed functions and urban bodies 18. States are meant to devolve them by law, and State Finance Commissions should set the money flows every five years. In practice SFCs are late and under-resourced, so local bodies depend on State discretion.

Own revenue is thin. Property tax collects around 0.15 to 0.2 percent of GDP, user charges sit below cost and municipal bonds are small. Local governments spend about 5 percent of all public expenditure, against 25 to 40 percent in comparable democracies.

key_terms.meaning: Panchayati Raj Institution, the rural local body.
Urban Local Body, such as a municipal corporation.
State Finance Commission under Art. 243-I and 243-Y.
Functions, finances and functionaries not matching on paper.
Debt issued by an ULB under SEBI Regulations 2015.

worked_example.title: What weak collection costs a city
worked_example.setup: Illustrative city that assesses ₹200 crore of property tax. The deck puts collection efficiency at 40 to 70 percent, and OECD property tax at 1.1% of GDP against India's 0.15 to 0.2%.
steps: At 40 percent collection: 200 × 0.4 = 80.
At 70 percent collection: 200 × 0.7 = 140.
Uncollected at the low end: 200 − 80 = 120.
OECD against India's upper figure: 1.1 ÷ 0.2 = 5.5, so at least 5.5 times.
worked_example.answer: The city collects ₹80 to 140 crore of ₹200 crore, and the OECD average is at least 5.5 times India's property tax share of GDP.

mistakes: Reading devolution on paper as devolution in practice. Finances and functionaries lag.
Assuming bonds can fill the gap. Total issuance is under ₹5,000 crore and most ULBs lack audited accounts.
Skipping State Finance Commissions. Central FC grants to local bodies depend on SFCs being constituted.

recall.q: How many functions do the Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules list?
recall.a: 29 for panchayats and 18 for urban bodies.

recall.q: What does the 3F gap stand for?
recall.a: Functions, finances and functionaries.

recall.q: How often should an SFC be constituted?
recall.a: Every five years.

recall.q: What is India's property tax as a share of GDP?
recall.a: About 0.15 to 0.2 percent.

recall.q: Which city issued the first major municipal bond after 2015?
recall.a: Pune, in 2017 for ₹200 crore.

sections.title: Public Expenditure, Where the Money Goes
sections.big_idea: About **70 percent of Union spending is already committed**, so the real choices sit in a narrow slice.
in_plain_words: Interest, transfers to States, defence, subsidies and pensions take roughly 70 percent of Union expenditure. Interest alone is about 24 percent and about 40 percent of revenue receipts, so debt service is paid before any new choice is made.

Within what remains, the deck traces the subsidy system, the big schemes, a capex push and a long under-investment in health and education. Composition matters as much as level. Ask what kind of capex and which part of a sector's share goes to salaries.

key_terms.meaning: Spending fixed by earlier choices or law, such as interest.
Spending that creates assets; rose to about 22% of spending.
Debt service or borrowing leaves less room for other uses.
Direct Benefit Transfer, which converts some subsidies to cash.
Change in debt equals (r − g) times debt, minus primary surplus.

worked_example.title: How much is left to decide?
worked_example.setup: Use the low-end shares on slide 57 for the five committed heads, then apply the interest figure from slide 63.
steps: Interest, transfers and defence: 24 + 22 + 13 = 59.
Add subsidies at the low end: 59 + 7 = 66.
Add pensions: 66 + 6 = 72.
What is left: 100 − 72 = 28, close to the slide's 30 percent.
If interest is 40 percent of revenue receipts and receipts are ₹100: 100 × 0.4 = 40.
worked_example.answer: About 72 percent is committed and about 28 percent is open, which matches the slide's rough 70 and 30. Interest alone commits ₹40 of every ₹100 of revenue receipts.

mistakes: Reading the headline allocation for a sector as the whole picture. The composition inside it is where design happens.
Applauding a capex rise without asking where. Social-sector capex has not accelerated like roads and rail.
Treating PM-KISAN as a subsidy. The slide calls it technically an income transfer.

recall.q: Which is the largest single Union expenditure head?
recall.a: Interest payments, about 24 percent.

recall.q: What was public health spending as a share of GDP and its target?
recall.a: About 1.9 percent against a 2.5 percent target.

recall.q: What happened to Union capex between 2018-19 and 2024-25 BE?
recall.a: It rose from about ₹3 lakh crore to about ₹11 lakh crore.

recall.q: What was out-of-pocket health spending in 2021-22?
recall.a: 39.4 percent of total health expenditure.

recall.q: Why does r above g matter?
recall.a: Debt grows even with a balanced primary budget.

sections.title: Gender, Caste & Outcome Budgeting
sections.big_idea: Headline aggregates show what a government noticed. **Disaggregated statements show who it was thinking about.**
in_plain_words: The Union Budget carries separate statements for gender, SC and ST sub-plans and children. Each reports allocations, and each is better at tracking outputs than outcomes. The gender statement splits schemes into Part A and Part B and the 30 percent claim in Part B is not externally audited.

Outcome budgeting asks for changes in people's lives, but the data systems often cannot supply them. Participatory budgeting, such as Kerala's People's Plan, works at sub-State scale. Always ask whether an allocation was ever traced to a changed outcome.

key_terms.meaning: Schemes fully for women / with at least 30% benefit to women.
SC and Tribal Sub-Plans, aiming at population-share allocations.
Immediate measurable result, such as schools built.
The change the spending should bring, such as learning levels.
Citizens take part in deciding spending, as in Kerala since 1996.

worked_example.title: Targets and shares
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a ₹1,000 crore pool of divisible scheme funds, with the SC and ST targets from slide 67. Then children's share of population against spending.
steps: SC target at 16.6 percent: 1,000 × 0.166 = 166.
ST target at 8.6 percent: 1,000 × 0.086 = 86.
Children are about 36 percent of the population and the child budget is about 3 percent of Union spending.
Population share against spending share: 36 ÷ 3 = 12.
worked_example.answer: The targets would be about ₹166 crore for SCs and ₹86 crore for STs. Children's population share is 12 times their share of Union spending.

mistakes: Reading an output as an outcome. Schools opened do not show learning gains.
Adding up Part B allocations as money spent on women. The 30 percent benefit claim is unaudited.
Assuming notional SC and ST allocations reach those groups. The deck lists diversion and unspent balances.

recall.q: When was the Gender Budget Statement introduced?
What are the SCSP and TSP targets?
recall.a: About 16.6 percent for SCs and about 8.6 percent for STs.

recall.q: Who advocated for the child budget statement?
recall.a: HAQ Centre for Child Rights and partners, from 2008-09.

recall.q: When was the Output-Outcome Framework reintroduced?
What share of plan funds does Kerala's People's Plan devolve?
recall.a: About 35 to 40 percent.

sections.title: Public Debt, Deficit & Macro Stability
sections.big_idea: Debt is a bet on growth: **the gap between interest rate r and growth g** decides whether the debt ratio rises or falls.
in_plain_words: General government debt is about 83 percent of GDP and mostly rupee-denominated, held by banks, insurers and provident funds. The change in the debt ratio equals (r minus g) times the ratio, minus the primary surplus. If r exceeds g, debt rises even with a balanced primary budget.

Off-budget borrowings, guarantees and pension liabilities sit outside the headline. RBI and the Treasury coordinate under an inflation target, and sovereign ratings set a ceiling on external borrowing costs. India's rating is at the lower end of investment grade.

diagram.note: an approximation, so check units and whether figures are nominal

key_terms.meaning: Effective interest rate on government debt.
Nominal GDP growth.
Fiscal surplus excluding interest; a primary deficit counts as negative.
A commitment, such as a guarantee, that may become a cost.
Monetary Policy Committee with a 4 percent target and a band of 2 points.

worked_example.title: Does the debt ratio fall?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative, using the deck's ranges: debt 83% of GDP, r of 7.5%, g of 10%, and a primary deficit of 1.4% of GDP (so the primary surplus is −1.4).
steps: Gap between r and g: 7.5 − 10 = −2.5 points.
Gap times debt ratio: 2.5 × 0.83 = 2.075, which pulls the ratio down by about 2.1 points.
The primary deficit adds back 1.4 points.
Net change: 2.075 − 1.4 = 0.675, a fall of about 0.7 points of GDP.
worked_example.answer: The debt ratio falls by about 0.7 points a year on these figures, provided growth stays above the interest rate.

mistakes: Quoting one rating for all three agencies. S&P is BBB, Moody's Baa3 and Fitch BBB-.
Reading headline deficit and debt as the whole liability. Off-budget borrowings and guarantees sit outside.
Assuming favourable arithmetic lasts. The deck says the hard part is sustaining growth and a moderate primary deficit together.

recall.q: What is general government debt as a share of GDP?
recall.a: About 83 percent.

recall.q: What happens if r exceeds g?
recall.a: The debt ratio rises even with a balanced primary budget.

recall.q: What was the CAG's 2018 finding on off-budget liabilities?
recall.a: About ₹1.5 lakh crore of undisclosed off-budget liabilities.

recall.q: What is India's inflation target?
recall.a: 4 percent, with a band of 2 points either way.

recall.q: Why does the sovereign rating matter?
recall.a: It sets a ceiling for Indian corporates borrowing abroad and affects portfolio inflows.

sections.title: Reading a Budget: A Practitioner's Toolkit
sections.big_idea: Read in a fixed order: **Budget at a Glance, then the Demand for Grants**, then the receipts and statements, then the outcome framework.
in_plain_words: Start with Budget at a Glance for the headline numbers within a day. Go to the Demand for Grants for your scheme and compare BE, RE and actuals over three years. The gap between BE and actuals tells you whether a scheme has implementation bottlenecks.

Use the Receipt Budget to test whether revenue assumptions look realistic. Then use the statements for cross-cutting analysis and the Output-Outcome Framework for results. State budgets follow the same pattern. A small network of organisations publishes free analysis.

diagram.caption: the reading order in this section

key_terms.meaning: Budget Estimate, the amount planned for the coming year.
Revised Estimate, the mid-year update for the current year.
What was spent or received in the closed year.
Detailed breakdown of all receipt heads.
Scheme-wise outputs and outcomes, published separately since 2017-18.

worked_example.title: Spot a scheme with a bottleneck
worked_example.setup: Illustrative scheme in ₹ crore: BE 1,000, RE 900 and actuals 780 for the closed year. Apply the under-spending diagnostic from slide 82.
steps: Gap between BE and actuals: 1,000 − 780 = 220.
As a share of BE: 220 ÷ 1,000 = 0.22, which is 22 percent.
Gap between RE and actuals: 900 − 780 = 120.
Repeat for the two earlier years. A high BE with persistently lower actuals points to implementation bottlenecks.
worked_example.answer: The scheme under-spent its BE by 22 percent. One year proves little, so check whether the gap repeats.

mistakes: Reading only the Budget Speech. The Demand for Grants holds the scheme detail.
Comparing a scheme across one year only. The slide asks for three years of BE, RE and actuals.
Quoting statement numbers from memory. This deck gives different numbers on different slides, so confirm in the document.

recall.q: How many pages is Budget at a Glance, roughly?
recall.a: About 30 pages.

recall.q: What does the under-spending diagnostic say?
recall.a: A high BE with persistently lower actuals points to implementation bottlenecks.

recall.q: Which organisation publishes a Budget Highlights summary within 24 hours?
recall.a: PRS Legislative Research.

recall.q: What are the three tests for an outcome indicator?
recall.a: Whether it is a real outcome or a proxy, whether the target is ambitious, and whether independent data can verify it.

recall.q: How long does the deck suggest to build a working understanding of one State?
recall.a: Around two days.

sections.title: Further Reading & Glossary
sections.big_idea: Use the sources and the **four-question public-finance test**: money source, appropriation chain, budget head and accountability.
in_plain_words: This section lists primary sources, scholarly works and data sources. Primary texts are free: the budget documents, Economic Survey, RBI reports, Finance Commission reports and CAG audits. The glossary groups the terms in three parts: budget mechanics, federalism and taxes, and debt and institutions.

Three data-visualisation slides close the section: the Union budget flow, the debt comparison with peers and the tax-to-GDP and deficit charts. Ask the four questions of every proposal. The deck says a proposal silent on any one of them is not fiscally serious.

key_terms.meaning: Source, appropriation chain, budget head and accountability.
Receipt Budget statement of guarantees given by the Government of India.
Public Financial Management System for real-time fund tracking.
Borrowing through PSUs or the Public Account outside the headline deficit.
Flow chart that sizes bands by amount.

worked_example.title: Read the Sankey and test a proposal
worked_example.setup: The FY24 Sankey on slide 98 shows ₹10.2 lakh crore going to States out of ₹33.3 lakh crore of gross tax revenue. Then apply the four questions to an invented proposal.
steps: States' share: 10.2 ÷ 33.3 = 0.306, about 31 percent as the slide says.
Invented proposal: a new rural clinic scheme funded by borrowing.
Source: borrowing. Allocation: the Union, appropriated through a Demand for Grants.
Budget head: a Centrally Sponsored Scheme. Accountability: output indicators, with NFHS to verify outcomes.
worked_example.answer: States get about 31 percent of gross tax revenue in the diagram. The invented proposal passes because it names a source, an appropriation, a scheme head and an audit route.

mistakes: Reading the closing framings as statistics. They are the deck's summaries and reasoning.
Assuming the glossary replaces the articles. Each term points to a legal source worth reading.
Using the Sankey's 20 percent for interest without noting that other slides give about 24 percent.

recall.q: What are the four questions of the public-finance test?
recall.a: Where the money comes from, who allocates and appropriates, through which budget head and scheme, and how success is measured and audited.

recall.q: Which Act replaces the Income Tax Act, 1961?
recall.a: The Income Tax Act, 2025, from 1 April 2026.

recall.q: Name two sources of fiscal data from the deck.
recall.a: Any two of indiabudget.gov.in, the RBI Handbook, RBI State Finances, CAG, PFMS, ebudget.gov.in.

recall.q: Which Finance Commission reports does the deck list?
recall.a: The 15th and the 16th, which was tabled in February 2026.

recall.q: What licence do the ImpactMojo courses carry?
recall.a: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

notes.2: This agenda is your **map of the twelve sections**. Sections 1 to 3 build the vocabulary and the budget process, 4 to 7 cover taxes and the three tiers of government, and 8 to 10 cover spending, equity budgets and debt. Section 11 is the practical toolkit, so go there first if you need to read a budget this week.
notes.4: Take the test on this slide **literally**. Pick one programme you work on and try to name its budget head, last year's releases and the demand for grants where it sits. Whichever of the three you cannot name is the gap between you and the actual policy. Fix that gap before you form an opinion.
notes.5: Remember the three functions as **allocate, redistribute, stabilise**. The part to keep is the warning at the bottom: one decision usually does all three, as the food subsidy example shows. When you analyse a measure, ask which function it serves first and which others it serves as well, and avoid giving it a single label.
notes.6: Use this slide as a **checklist of reasons for public spending**. A good counts as public only if it is both non-rival and non-excludable, so test both words before you use the label. The closing paragraph tells you where the real argument lies: which interventions, at what scale and with what design.
notes.7: Read each row of the table for **who provides, who pays and who regulates**. PMJAY shows the mix: the public pays and private hospitals deliver. The slide names four roles for the state: direct provider, payer, regulator and absent. When you cost a sector, count all four, including what the state chose to leave undone.
notes.8: Here the deck states its method: a budget is a **political document written in numbers**, so the institutional detail is the substance. Keep the promised outcome in front of you as you read. By the end you should be able to read Budget at a Glance, find a scheme in the Demand for Grants and say who finances what.
notes.10: Do not try to memorise every article. Learn the **clusters**. Articles 110 to 117 govern how the Union Budget moves through Parliament, 202 to 207 repeat that for States, and 265 and 266 say where tax authority and public money sit. Article 280 creates the Finance Commission and Article 293 limits State borrowing.
notes.11: Picture three containers. The **Consolidated Fund** holds almost all revenue and needs Parliament's appropriation to spend. The **Public Account** holds money the government keeps as banker, such as provident funds. The Contingency Fund is a reserve for surprises. Charged items sit inside the first container and are debated but cannot be voted down.
notes.12: The CAG checks **after the money is spent**. Remember three audit types: financial for correctness, compliance for legality and performance for the three Es. The limits matter as much as the powers, because recommendations are not binding and committee follow-up is described as weak. Treat a CAG report as strong evidence with uncertain consequences.
notes.13: Sort every rupee of receipt into **tax, non-tax, borrowing or non-debt capital**. The warning sits in the last paragraph: borrowing creates a future obligation, so adding it beside tax revenue overstates what the government has. The slide calls this the most common practitioner error. When you see a receipts total, ask how much of it is borrowed.
notes.14: Use one question to split spending: **does it build an asset or reduce a liability?** If yes it is capital expenditure, and if no it is revenue expenditure. Then locate any scheme by walking down the hierarchy from function to department to major head to object head. The capex share of total spending is one signal of fiscal quality.
notes.15: Learn the deficits as a ladder of **ever wider borrowing**. Revenue deficit shows borrowing for running costs, fiscal deficit is the total borrowing need, and primary deficit strips out interest on past debt. Read all three together. A high fiscal deficit with a low primary deficit means most new borrowing services old debt.
notes.16: Four questions open any budget document: **which fund, which authority, which receipt category, and how the deficits move**. Memorise them as your first pass before you read a single scheme line. The slide says they cover most of what you need, so use them as your standing opening routine.
notes.18: Follow the year as **eight steps**: circular, estimates, consultations, presentation on 1 February, scrutiny, passage by 31 March, execution and audit. Match your advocacy to the step. Pre-Budget consultations in December and January happen before the figures are fixed, so that is the moment to send a submission.
notes.19: Do not try to read every document. Start with **Budget at a Glance**, then go to the Demands for Grants for scheme detail, since those are what Lok Sabha votes. The Finance Bill carries tax proposals and the Appropriation Bill gives legal authority to withdraw money. All are free at indiabudget.gov.in.
notes.20: Standing committees are where **detailed scrutiny** happens, so use them. Twenty-four committees shadow the Ministries, meet in private, publish their reports and accept written memoranda from civil society. If you work in health, education or rural development, read your committee's latest report before you read news coverage.
notes.21: Four procedures handle money outside the normal path: Vote on Account, supplementary, excess and token demands. Learn what **triggers** each one. Frequent large supplementary demands on one head are a signal, according to the slide, of poor estimation or of a scheme growing without primary debate.
notes.22: Track the FRBM story as **promise, breach, reset**. The 2003 targets were revised and breached, the 2018 amendment moved to a debt anchor of 40 percent for the Centre and 60 percent combined, and the escape clause was used in the COVID year when the deficit passed 9.2 percent. India still has no independent Fiscal Council.
notes.23: Hold two scores together: India gets 51 out of 100 on budget transparency but **6 on public participation**. Documents are public and citizens have little formal voice. The deck calls that gap your opportunity space. Study the list of things hidden from view, such as off-budget borrowings.
notes.24: This slide lists the **entry points for advocacy**: pre-Budget submissions, memoranda to committees, post-Budget analysis and tracking during the year. Pick the one that fits your capacity and time. Knowing the cycle, the slide says, is half the work. Section 4 now turns to how the state raises revenue.
notes.26: Direct taxes fall on the person who pays them, while indirect taxes are **passed on through prices**. That is why the mix matters for fairness: the poor spend a larger share of income on consumption. Check the numbers too. India's tax-GDP ratio is about 17 to 18 percent, far below Brazil and the OECD average.
notes.27: Most people who file pay little, and a **small group of high earners** pays most of the income tax. The slide says about 70 percent of filers reported zero or negligible liability. So the main lever it names is widening the base: better detection, formalising informal income and cutting exemptions.
notes.28: GST is a **shared tax** run by the Centre and States through the GST Council. Remember the vote rule: the Centre holds one-third of the weight, States two-thirds, and decisions need three-fourths. Neither side can pass a decision alone. Note the 2025 change to rates of 0, 5 and 18 percent plus a 40 percent rate.
notes.29: The 2019 cut from 30 to 22 percent cost about ₹1.45 lakh crore of revenue in the first year, by the CBDT estimate. Whether it **paid for itself** is contested. On Pillar Two, follow the slide's own advice: check the latest Finance Act before you say whether it applies.
notes.30: Cess and surcharge are the Centre's way to raise revenue **outside the pool shared with States**. Their share of gross tax revenue rose from about 10 percent to over 20 percent. When you read a devolution figure, ask how much of the Centre's tax take never entered the pool at all.
notes.31: Use the chart to see that the ratio has been **flat for two decades** at 16 to 18 percent. Then do the arithmetic the slide invites: a rise of two to three points would add ₹6 to 9 lakh crore a year. The slide calls the obstacle political.
notes.32: Each cause of the narrow base has a constituency, which is why reform is slow. The informal economy, the agricultural income exemption, weak property tax and the end of wealth tax all hold revenue down. Skim the reform list and notice that **official committees have recommended most of it** for decades.
notes.33: Treat this slide as your reason to ask about revenue. Before you back any new spending, ask **where the money comes from**. The slide says the low ratio reflects a long political settlement in which each group protects something. Section 5 next shows how revenue is shared with States.
notes.35: Read the table by its middle column. The **Centre holds the richest tax bases**: income, corporate and customs. States hold alcohol, land revenue and agricultural income tax, which grow more slowly. That mismatch is why devolution exists. GST sits in the middle, levied under Articles 246A and 269A.
notes.36: Keep two questions apart. **Vertical** asks how much of the divisible pool goes to States in total, which was 42 percent under the 14th FC and 41 under the 15th. **Horizontal** asks how that share is split among States, using weighted criteria. The shift to 2011 population is the contested part.
notes.37: Memorise the arc: the 14th FC raised devolution to 42 percent, the 15th kept 41, and the 16th, whose report was tabled on 1 February 2026, holds it at 41 for 2026 to 31. The Commission's advice is not binding but is usually accepted. The Terms of Reference decide what it may examine.
notes.38: Read this as a story about **trust**. States gave up taxes in 2017 against a promise of compensation at 14 percent annual growth for five years. COVID widened the gap and the regime ended in June 2022. The slide's lesson: co-operative federalism under stress relies on the Centre's discretion.
notes.39: Learn both arguments before you choose one. The **equity** case says poorer States need more. The **performance** case says States that controlled population and raised revenue are penalised. The slide shows Tamil Nadu falling from 5.3 to 4.1 percent while Bihar rose to 10.1. It calls the debate constitutional, with the formulae second.
notes.40: A CSS is designed by the Centre, part-funded by both, and run by States. The usual ratios are 60:40 and 75:25, with **90:10 for the North-East** and J&K and Ladakh. The critique is that conditional money steers State priorities and uses up State funds. A Central Sector Scheme is fully Union-funded.
notes.41: Take away the asymmetry: the Centre has the revenue and the States have the delivery. The slide says the arrangement has held for seven decades because it is **renegotiated every five years**. Use the practitioner questions at the end whenever you design something at State level: whose subject, what funding, what fiscal room.
notes.43: Look at where a State's money comes from before you judge its choices. Devolution and central grants together form about **half of receipts**, so own revenue is limited. Alcohol excise and petroleum VAT are major own-revenue heads. Check your own State's mix in its budget.
notes.44: Article 293 gives the Union a **practical veto on State borrowing**, because States nearly always owe the Centre something. Each year the Centre sets a net borrowing ceiling. Off-budget borrowing was a workaround, and scrutiny tightened from 2022-23. Kerala's challenge before the Supreme Court is pending, so check its status.
notes.45: DISCOM losses reach State budgets through guarantees and debt takeovers. Under UDAY in 2015 States took over **75 percent of about ₹4.3 lakh crore** of debt. The slide says many returned to operating losses afterwards. Reform is technically clear and politically hard because free farm power is protected.
notes.46: Compare States on the **four stress markers**: persistent revenue deficit, interest above 15 percent of revenue receipts, a sharply rising pension burden and off-budget liabilities. A State showing all four is stressed whatever its headline ratio. Note the spread, from Maharashtra near 18 percent to Punjab at 46 percent.
notes.47: The pension choice is a decision whose **cost arrives decades later**. OPS pays a defined benefit linked to the last salary out of State budgets, while NPS depends on accumulated contributions. When a State reverts to OPS, the liability moves to future budgets. UPS 2024 is the Centre's hybrid, and States adopt it voluntarily.
notes.48: State cash-transfer schemes are now a major fiscal item. The slide notes they are electorally sticky and, at scale, can **crowd out capital spending**. Decide for yourself where welfare ends and freebie begins, using the RBI study the slide mentions, and find out which institutes track your State.
notes.49: Turn the closing advice into a **twenty-page habit**: the State Budget at a Glance, the MTFPS, the latest CAG audit and the RBI chapter for your State. The slide calls the gap between mandate and means permanent. Section 7 now goes below the State to local bodies.
notes.51: The 73rd and 74th Amendments wrote local bodies into the Constitution, listing 29 functions for panchayats and 18 for urban bodies. The idea to keep is the **3F gap**: functions moved on paper, while finances and functionaries did not. Check any local programme for all three Fs before you assume it can deliver.
notes.52: State Finance Commissions should do for local bodies what the Finance Commission does for States, every five years. In practice they are **late, irregular and selectively accepted**. Without them local bodies live on State discretion from year to year. Central FC grants to local bodies depend on SFCs being constituted.
notes.53: Property tax is the **underused lever**. India collects about 0.15 to 0.2 percent of GDP against about 1.1 percent in the OECD, and collection efficiency is often 40 to 70 percent. Every reform on the list (mapping, self-assessment, revaluation) carries a political cost that arrives immediately.
notes.54: Weigh each source by how real it is. Water and sewerage charges sit below cost, octroi vanished with GST, and **municipal bonds are small**, under ₹5,000 crore in total. Most ULBs lack the audited accounts that market access needs. Pune's ₹200 crore issue in 2017 was the first major one after 2015.
notes.55: The key figure is five percent: local governments spend about 5 percent of public expenditure where comparable democracies spend 25 to 40. The slide reads that gap as **the size of the unkept promise**. Keep it in mind when you judge any local programme. Section 8 follows the money that does flow.
notes.57: Read the table for what is **already committed**. Interest, transfers to States, defence, subsidies and pensions take about 70 percent of Union spending, leaving roughly 30 percent to decide each year. New programmes therefore compete in a narrower space than the headline suggests.
notes.58: Compare the instruments as well as the sums. The same goal can be met with a price subsidy, a cash transfer or free provision, and the slide says each has efficiency and equity trade-offs. Food is the largest line at about ₹2 lakh crore, and DBT has already replaced part of the LPG subsidy.
notes.59: Use the table as a **sense of scale**. The largest lines are MGNREGA and the two housing schemes, then Jal Jeevan Mission. Remember the slide's warning that the Centre:State ratio and eligibility rules decide delivery. Read the table's note on the MGNREGA replacement before you quote its figure.
notes.60: Capex more than tripled, from about ₹3 lakh crore to ₹11 lakh crore, and rose from about 12 to 22 percent of spending. The slide's critique concerns **composition**: roads, rail and defence gained while school buildings and primary health did not. Ask what kind of capex before you applaud.
notes.61: Defence is a case of **committed spending**. It takes about 13 percent of Union expenditure, with pensions rising and multi-year contracts that cannot be paused. The slide links the 2022 Agnipath reform to pension liability and compares it with the OPS-NPS debate you met in Section 6.
notes.62: Health and education sit below their targets: about 1.9 percent of GDP on health against a 2.5 percent goal, and 4.6 percent on education against 6. States carry most of the load, so **State stress becomes underfunding**. Out-of-pocket health spending was still 39.4 percent in 2021-22.
notes.63: Interest is the biggest single Union head, about 24 percent of spending and about 40 percent of revenue receipts. Think of it as a **bill paid before any choice is made**. The debt equation at the end shows why r above g makes debt grow even with a balanced primary budget.
notes.64: This closing slide gives the method: three years of trend, peer-State comparison, share of own resources and scheme-level composition. The headline share for your sector says little by itself. The **composition inside it**, capex against salary and scheme against establishment, is where design happens.
notes.66: The Gender Budget Statement describes allocations after the fact, and the budget process upstream is not gender-disaggregated. Part A holds schemes fully for women, Part B those with at least 30 percent benefit. Treat the **headline total with care**, since the 30 percent claim is not externally audited.
notes.67: Compare the target with the report. The SC Sub-Plan aims at about **16.6 percent** and the Tribal Sub-Plan at about 8.6 percent, matching population shares. The slide lists the gaps: notional allocations, no beneficiary identification and unspent balances. Andhra Pradesh and Telangana have the most developed legal framework.
notes.68: Children are about 36 percent of the population and the child budget is about 3 percent of Union spending. That is the **number to remember**. The statement tracks scheme allocations and their trend well, and misses State spending, capital spending and outcomes. Look to other data for results.
notes.69: Keep **output and outcome** apart. Schools built is an output, while learning levels is an outcome. The Output-Outcome Framework since 2017-18 mostly tracks outputs, because reliable outcome data is thin. Ask of any indicator whether it could be met without anyone being better off.
notes.70: This is a history of tools tried: performance budgeting in the late 1960s, zero-based budgeting abandoned in the late 1980s and now the Output-Outcome Framework. The **participatory examples** are Kerala's People's Plan, which devolved 35 to 40 percent of plan funds, and Pune. All run at sub-State scale.
notes.71: The slide's idea: aggregates show what a government noticed, and **disaggregation shows who it was thinking about**. Keep the list of statements handy for gender, child, SC and ST, and North East. Confirm statement numbers in the budget document itself, because this deck gives different numbers on different slides.
notes.73: General government debt is about 83 percent of GDP, with the Centre near 58 and States near 28. Most of it is **rupee-denominated and held at home**, which lowers currency risk. The rating sits at the lower end of investment grade, and the slide ties slow upgrades to debt, deficit and contingent liabilities.
notes.74: Use the equation as a quick test: the change in the debt ratio equals (r minus g) times the debt ratio, minus the primary surplus. **If r exceeds g, debt grows** even with a balanced primary budget. The slide says growth has run ahead of the interest rate in India, which gives room if growth holds.
notes.75: Headline numbers cover only the Consolidated Fund book. Check four hiding places: off-budget borrowings, guarantees, subsidy arrears and unfunded pensions. The slide records that FCI and NHAI borrowing were brought on book. A 2018 CAG report put undisclosed liabilities at about **₹1.5 lakh crore**.
notes.76: Split the roles. The Treasury sets fiscal policy, and RBI sets monetary policy against a 4 percent inflation target with a band of two points either side. Government appoints three of six MPC members. RBI's surplus transfer, ₹2 to 3 lakh crore, is a major **non-tax receipt**.
notes.77: The timeline is the lesson: coordination worked in 2008-09 and 2020-22 and slipped in 2010-13. The list at the bottom is a **decision table** that pairs each condition with a fiscal and monetary response. Use it to ask whether a government's policy mix fits the situation it faces.
notes.78: Know the three ratings: BBB at S&P after its August 2025 upgrade, Baa3 at Moody's and BBB- at Fitch. The slide gives a spread of 50 to 100 basis points between BBB- and BBB+ on external debt. Rating matters even with low external debt because **Indian corporates borrow abroad**.
notes.79: A one-line version: debt is **a bet on growth**. The slide closes the section with a practical point, that every spending proposal eventually becomes a debt question. Carry the interest burden forward as the arithmetic behind all earlier sections. Section 11 moves from analysis to reading documents.
notes.81: Read Budget at a Glance first, within a day of presentation. Use the **six first-pass questions** on the slide as your script: deficits, comparison with last year's BE and RE, top five heads, change in your scheme, capex share and the tax-GDP assumption. Then compare with the PRS and CBGA summaries.
notes.82: Find your scheme in the Demand for Grants, then compare **BE, RE and actuals** across three years. The diagnostic: a high BE with persistently lower actuals means implementation bottlenecks. A high BE that keeps rising without more output deserves scrutiny. For a CSS, check the Centre:State share.
notes.83: Read the Receipt Budget for **how realistic the revenue assumptions are**. Compare BE with RE for the same year, since persistent over-estimation of tax revenue is a known critique. Watch RBI dividend swings of up to ₹1 lakh crore, plus spectrum receipts and disinvestment, which distort the headline.
notes.84: Treat this table as a **finder**: one statement for subsidies, one for guarantees, two for functional and economic classification, and the cross-cutting statements for children, SC and ST, gender and the North East. The numbers differ from earlier slides, so confirm each one in the live document.
notes.85: Judge outcome indicators with three tests: is it a real outcome or a proxy, is the target ambitious, and can independent data verify it. The slide names NFHS, ASER and PLFS as the actual outcome sources. The framework runs past 200 pages and its quality varies by Ministry.
notes.86: State budgets mirror the Union structure under Article 202. Plan about **two days** for a working understanding of one State: its latest budget, latest CAG audit, MTFPS and the RBI State Finances chapter. The slide says that base lasts a year. RTI requests help with sub-State data.
notes.87: You do not need ten sources. Follow **four or five** consistently, one per job: CBGA for sectoral analysis, CPR for scheme briefs, PRS for 24-hour summaries, NIPFP and RBI for research and data. Most outputs are free, so the only cost is your time.
notes.88: Here is a **rhythm for the year**: Budget at a Glance on day 1, the PRS summary on day 2, CBGA within the week, CPR briefs within the month, then committee and CAG reports as they appear. The slide puts the total at about twelve hours a year.
notes.90: Bookmark by type: constitutional and statutory texts, annual official documents and committee reports. Finance Commission reports run 300 to 500 pages, so read the **executive summary first**, a one-day task. The Income Tax Act, 2025 replaces the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026.
notes.91: Use the reading list in layers. Start with Musgrave for the frame, Wildavsky and Schick for how budgets work in politics, then the Indian classics by Datta, Rao, Sen and Bagchi, then current writers. Choose **one book and one journal** from the list and follow them for a year.
notes.92: Know where the data lives: indiabudget.gov.in for budget documents, the RBI for time series and State Finances, CAG for audits and PFMS for real-time scheme funds. Most are free. Indiastat.com and CMIE Economic Outlook are **subscription services**, so check access before you plan around them.
notes.93: This slide points to flagship courses and companion 101 courses. Choose by your gap: MEL if you need to judge outcomes, Gender Studies for the frame behind gender budgeting, DataViz and DevAI for working with budget data. All courses are free and carry a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 licence.
notes.94: Use the glossary to test yourself: cover the right-hand column and define each term in one sentence. Start with the **three public-money containers** and the three deficits. Notice that every core term carries its article number, which doubles as a pointer to the legal source.
notes.95: These terms fit one chain: cess and surcharge stay outside the divisible pool, the Finance Commission splits the pool, and the GST Council makes joint decisions. Test yourself on **vertical against horizontal**, and on CSS against Central Sector Scheme. The 41 percent figure belongs to the 15th FC.
notes.96: Part 3 groups debt and institutions. OPS, NPS and UPS form a sequence of pension designs, and the **3F gap** is the one phrase that sums up local government weakness. Crowding-out means government borrowing raises interest rates or absorbs financial resources, which reduces private investment.
notes.97: This closing framing says public finance is a discipline of public reason, so the case for any allocation has to be made in public. The practical claim concerns the Constitution: the slide says the fiscal articles carry **as much weight as the rights articles** in shaping how the state operates.
notes.98: The Sankey summarises the budget rupee for FY24. Read the right side first: **interest takes about 20 percent** of total expenditure in this diagram, the largest head. States receive about 31 percent of gross tax revenue here, 10.2 of 33.3 lakh crore. Borrowing finances roughly a third.
notes.99: Compare India with its peers on two features of the chart: the rise at COVID and the plateau near 80 percent. India sits above most emerging-market peers and well below Japan. The slide says the **60 percent FRBM target** was breached before COVID, so the glide path remains contested.
notes.100: Use the four questions as a **filter on any proposal**: where the money comes from, who allocates and appropriates, which budget head and scheme type carries it, and how success will be measured and audited. By the slide's test, a proposal silent on any one of them is not fiscally serious.
notes.101: This slide closes the deck's argument: reading a budget well is a form of citizenship. The deck calls its 104 slides a beginning. The work it describes is slow, one budget, one scheme and one CAG report at a time. Plan your yearly reading rhythm from Section 11.
notes.102: Use the bar chart as a **comparison anchor**: India at about 17.8 percent against an OECD average near 34. The slide calls this the structural constraint, since more social spending without more revenue means more debt. Pair it with the two-decade chart on slide 31 before you quote either.
notes.103: The chart shows combined Centre and State deficits: about 6.5 percent of GDP in the 2010s, near 13 percent in 2020-21 and slow consolidation since. The target is 3 percent each, 6 combined. India is **structurally above target**, so room for counter-cyclical spending is narrow.
